exhibits.title: Memory Room
exhibits.subtitle: The cognitive architecture of encoding, consolidation, storage, and retrieval
exhibits.curatorQuote: Memory is not a static recording played back from a disc; every time a memory is recalled, it is actively reconstructed and re-encoded.
exhibits.description: Step into the deep vault of human memory. Deconstruct how fleeting electrical activity in synapses becomes structural biological connections, examine why our working memory is capped at a few discrete units, and explore how ancient mnemonic palaces allow extraordinary feats of recall.

sections.name: Working Memory
sections.description: Baddeley and Hitch's multi-component model shows that working memory is an active mental workspace rather than a passive holding pen. It consists of the Central Executive, the Phonological Loop (inner voice), the Visuospatial Sketchpad (inner eye), and the Episodic Buffer.
keyPoints: Central Executive coordinates attention and suppresses irrelevant distractors.
Phonological Loop retains acoustic and verbal information through subvocal rehearsal.
Visuospatial Sketchpad manipulates visual and spatial representations.
Capacity is typically limited to 3-4 information chunks when active manipulation is required.

sections.name: Short-Term Memory
sections.description: George Miller's landmark 1956 finding revealed that human immediate span is approximately 7 ± 2 items (modern cognitive research estimates 4-5 discrete units without rehearsal). Without active rehearsal, short-term memory traces degrade within 15 to 30 seconds due to decay and interference.
keyPoints: Miller's Law (7 ± 2 items) can be significantly expanded using strategic 'chunking'.
Chunking groups raw stimuli (e.g. 1-9-8-4-2-0-0-1) into meaningful higher-order units (1984, 2001).
Peterson & Peterson (1959) showed rapid decay occurs if rehearsal is blocked by backward counting.

sections.name: Long-Term Memory
sections.description: Long-term memory branches into Explicit (Declarative) memory—which includes Episodic (autobiographical events) and Semantic (factual knowledge)—and Implicit (Non-declarative) memory—including Procedural skills (riding a bike) and emotional conditioning.
keyPoints: Long-Term Potentiation (LTP) strengthens synaptic transmission across the hippocampus and cortex.
Ebbinghaus's Forgetting Curve demonstrates that ~70% of new unreviewed data is lost within 24 hours.
Spaced repetition flattens the forgetting curve and accelerates synaptic consolidation.
Elizabeth Loftus demonstrated the 'Misinformation Effect'—memories are malleable and can be rewritten.

sections.name: Memory Games
sections.description: Interactive neuro-cognitive training modules designed to measure and challenge your Working Memory span and spatial recall capacity under varying interference conditions.
keyPoints: Spatial Span Memory Matrix: Replicate flashing tile grids of increasing complexity.
Digit Span Forward & Backward: Challenge your phonological loop capacity.
Method of Loci (Memory Palace) Interactive Walkthrough.

thoughtExperiment.title: The Lost in the Mall Experiment (Elizabeth Loftus)
thoughtExperiment.scenario: Psychologist Elizabeth Loftus presented participants with four childhood stories from their families. Three were true; one was completely fabricated: getting lost in a shopping mall at age five and crying until comforted by an elderly stranger.
thoughtExperiment.takeaway: Over 25% of participants began 'remembering' rich sensory details of the fake event, proving memories are dynamically reconstructed rather than retrieved as immutable video recordings.

quiz.question: According to Baddeley's model, which component of working memory is responsible for manipulating visual and spatial images?
quiz.explanation: The Visuospatial Sketchpad acts as the brain's 'inner eye', responsible for holding and manipulating spatial and visual information.

quiz.question: What did George Miller's classic 1956 research identify as the magical span of immediate short-term memory?
quiz.explanation: George Miller's landmark paper established that immediate short-term memory can typically hold 7 ± 2 items or chunks.

quiz.question: Which brain structure was famously demonstrated by Patient H.M. to be crucial for forming new declarative memories?
quiz.explanation: After bilateral removal of his medial temporal lobes including the hippocampus, Patient H.M. could no longer form new episodic or semantic long-term memories.

quiz.question: What is the primary way to prevent the rapid forgetting shown in Ebbinghaus's Forgetting Curve?
quiz.explanation: Spaced retrieval practice strengthens synaptic consolidation and systematically flattens the rate of forgetting over time.

exhibits.title: Emotion Room
exhibits.subtitle: The evolutionary symphony of the limbic system, affective appraisal, and somatic feelings
exhibits.curatorQuote: Emotions are not irrational disruptions to cognition; they are ancient evolutionary heuristics forged over millions of years to guarantee survival.
exhibits.description: Explore the evolutionary matrix of feeling. Traverse Robert Plutchik's 3D emotional wheel, dissect micro-expressions that escape conscious masking, explore how bodily physiology influences your conscious mood, and test your emotional intelligence (EQ).

sections.name: Human Emotions
sections.description: From William James to modern neuroscience, emotion theory traces how physiological sensations produce affect. Robert Plutchik's Wheel of Emotions identifies 8 primary emotional vectors (Joy, Trust, Fear, Surprise, Sadness, Disgust, Anger, Anticipation) that blend together into complex secondary and tertiary states.
keyPoints: Plutchik's vectors blend like primary colors (Joy + Trust = Love; Fear + Surprise = Awe).
James-Lange Theory: Bodily arousal occurs first, and the brain interprets the arousal as emotion ('We feel sorry because we cry').
Schachter-Singer Two-Factor Theory: Emotion = Physiological Arousal + Cognitive Appraisal label.
Lisa Feldman Barrett's Constructed Emotion: Emotions are constructed predictions, not hard-wired reactive circuits.

sections.name: Facial Expressions
sections.description: Dr. Paul Ekman's worldwide cross-cultural studies in Papua New Guinea demonstrated that six basic facial expressions are biologically universal rather than culturally learned: Happiness, Sadness, Fear, Anger, Surprise, and Disgust (later adding Contempt).
keyPoints: Facial Action Coding System (FACS) maps all 43 facial muscle movements into Action Units (AUs).
Micro-expressions flash in 1/25th to 1/5th of a second when an individual attempts to conceal an emotion.
Duchenne smile engages the orbicularis oculi muscle ('crow's feet' around the eyes), distinguishing genuine joy from fake polite smiles.

sections.name: Emotional Intelligence
sections.description: Salovey, Mayer, and Daniel Goleman formulated Emotional Intelligence (EQ) as the capacity to recognize, understand, manage, and harness emotions in oneself and others. Damasio's Somatic Marker hypothesis showed that without emotional feedback, rational decision-making collapses.
keyPoints: Four Pillars: Self-Awareness, Self-Regulation, Social Awareness (Empathy), and Relationship Management.
Amygdala Hijacking: When intense stress causes the amygdala to trigger fight-or-flight before the prefrontal cortex can assess context.
Cognitive Empathy (perspective-taking) vs Affective Empathy (feeling another's pain).

sections.name: Interactive Activities
sections.description: Hands-on affective labs: Examine the interactive Plutchik Emotion Wheel, test your micro-expression recognition reflex, and engage in the Vagus-pacing autonomic breathing biofeedback simulation.
keyPoints: Plutchik 3D Color Wheel Explorer: Blend emotions and discover dynamic pairings.
Micro-Expression Flash Test: Identify subtle emotions under time pressure.
Vagus Nerve 4-7-8 Breathing Pacer: Regulate parasympathetic nervous system tone.

thoughtExperiment.title: The Suspension Bridge Experiment (Dutton & Aron, 1974)
thoughtExperiment.scenario: Young men crossed either a terrifying, swaying 230-foot suspension bridge or a safe cedar bridge. An attractive female researcher approached them with a questionnaire and her phone number. Far more men from the suspension bridge called her asking for a date.
thoughtExperiment.takeaway: The brain frequently misattributes autonomic physiological arousal (racing pulse and adrenaline from danger) as romantic attraction—illustrating cognitive appraisal of emotional states.

quiz.question: Which facial muscle movement characterizes a genuine 'Duchenne smile' versus a posed polite smile?
options: Contraction of orbicularis oculi muscles crinkling the eyes
quiz.explanation: A genuine Duchenne smile involuntarily contracts the orbicularis oculi muscles around the outer eyes, creating distinctive 'crow's feet'.

quiz.question: According to Robert Plutchik's Wheel of Emotions, what primary emotion blends with 'Joy' to form 'Love'?
quiz.explanation: In Plutchik's model, the primary dyads consist of adjacent emotions; Joy plus Trust yields the primary blend of Love.

quiz.question: What term describes the sudden emotional takeover where the amygdala triggers fight-or-flight before the prefrontal cortex intervenes?
quiz.explanation: Coined by Daniel Goleman, 'Amygdala Hijack' refers to immediate emotional reactions that bypass slower cortical evaluation.

quiz.question: How long does a true facial micro-expression typically last on the human face?
quiz.explanation: Micro-expressions are fleeting involuntary facial movements that flash in a fraction of a second (1/25 to 1/5 of a second).

exhibits.title: Perception Room
exhibits.subtitle: Optical illusions, sensory gating, and how the brain hallucinates reality
exhibits.curatorQuote: We do not see the world as it actually is; we see a controlled top-down hallucination constrained by sensory input.
exhibits.description: Step into the sensory engine room. Your eyes transmit inverted 2D electrical pulses, yet your brain weaves a seamless, stabilized 3D panorama. Discover optical illusions that reveal where the brain's shortcuts slip, master Gestalt organizational laws, and take the famous Stroop Effect test.

sections.name: Optical Illusions
sections.description: Optical illusions are not failures of vision; they are proof that the visual cortex relies on top-down heuristics to guess depth, illumination, and geometry. Interactive exhibits feature the Müller-Lyer illusion, Kanizsa Triangle, Hermann Grid, and Café Wall illusion.
keyPoints: Müller-Lyer Illusion: Identical line lengths appear unequal due to arrowheads signaling inward vs outward perspective corners.
Kanizsa Triangle: The visual system generates illusory contours where none exist, completing familiar shapes automatically.
Hermann Grid: Dark illusory ghost spots appear at intersections due to lateral inhibition in retinal ganglion cells.
Café Wall Illusion: Parallel horizontal lines appear sloping due to alternating black-and-white tile luminance contrasts.

sections.name: Visual Perception
sections.description: Sensory organs receive 11 million bits of raw data per second, but conscious awareness processes merely 40-50 bits. Helmholtz described perception as 'Unconscious Inference'. The Gestalt School demonstrated that the whole is different from the sum of its parts.
keyPoints: Gestalt Principles: Proximity, Similarity, Continuity, Closure, and Figure-Ground segregation.
Depth Perception: Binocular cues (retinal disparity, convergence) combine with monocular cues (linear perspective, relative size, texture gradient).
Dorsal vs Ventral Stream: The 'Where/How' parietal pathway vs the 'What' temporal pathway.

sections.name: Brain Interpretation Exercises
sections.description: Experience the computational conflict between automatic reflexive processing and intentional executive control. Take the classic 1935 Stroop Test, examine the Thatcher Illusion, and experience inattentional blindness.
keyPoints: The Stroop Effect: Reading words is an automatic overlearned process that interferes with naming ink colors.
Inattentional Blindness: Simons and Chabris demonstrated 50% of people miss a person in a gorilla suit when counting basketball passes.
Thatcher Illusion: Inverted faces mask severe distortions because facial feature processing is orientation-specific.

thoughtExperiment.title: Mary the Color Scientist (Frank Jackson's Qualia Dilemma)
thoughtExperiment.scenario: Mary is a brilliant neuroscientist raised in a black-and-white room. She masters every physical, chemical, and neurological fact about color vision. One day, she steps outside and sees a ripe red apple for the first time. Does she learn anything new?
thoughtExperiment.takeaway: If Mary learns something new, physicalism is incomplete: subjective conscious experience ('qualia') cannot be purely reduced to objective neural equations.

quiz.question: Why do dark illusory spots appear at the white intersections of the Hermann Grid illusion?
options: Lateral inhibition among retinal ganglion cells
quiz.explanation: Lateral inhibition causes stimulated photoreceptors to diminish the activity of neighboring receptors, darkening intersections where inhibition is highest.

quiz.question: In the Stroop Effect test, what causes the delayed reaction time when reading the word 'BLUE' printed in red ink?
options: Cognitive conflict between automatic reading and deliberate color naming
quiz.explanation: Reading is an automatic, overlearned process that creates cognitive interference when you must consciously override it to name ink color.

quiz.question: Which Gestalt principle explains why your brain perceives a complete white triangle in the Kanizsa illusion even though no outline is drawn?
quiz.explanation: The principle of Closure causes the brain to fill in visual gaps to perceive familiar, complete, coherent shapes.

quiz.question: Which visual cortical stream is known as the 'Where / How' pathway?
quiz.explanation: The Dorsal Stream projecting into the parietal lobe processes spatial location, motion, and guiding motor action ('Where/How').

exhibits.title: Personality Room
exhibits.subtitle: The Big Five traits, psychometric assessment, and archetypes of the self
exhibits.curatorQuote: Personality is neither pure biology nor pure culture; it is the enduring pattern of thoughts, feelings, and behaviors that distinguish each human.
exhibits.description: Stand before the multidimensional mirror of human disposition. Unpack the scientific taxonomy of personality traits, complete an interactive Big Five OCEAN self-assessment with live radar chart visualization, and explore Jungian archetypes and the modern critique of MBTI.

sections.name: Personality Traits
sections.description: Scientific trait theory originated through the Lexical Hypothesis: important human behavioral differences become encoded into everyday language over generations. Modern psychometrics centers upon the robust Big Five (OCEAN) model.
keyPoints: Openness to Experience: Intellectual curiosity, artistic appreciation, unconventional thinking.
Conscientiousness: Self-discipline, organization, goal-directed persistence, impulse control.
Extraversion: Sociability, assertiveness, positive emotionality, sensitivity to rewards.
Agreeableness: Compassion, trust, cooperation, empathy versus antagonism.
Neuroticism: Emotional instability, anxiety, vulnerability to stress, negative affectivity.

sections.name: Self-Assessment Quiz
sections.description: Take the validated Big Five Mini-IPIP psychometric assessment directly inside the museum exhibit. Receive an immediate breakdown across all 5 dimensions plotted on an interactive holographic radar chart.
keyPoints: Calibrated 10-item psychometric assessment with balanced positive and reverse-keyed items.
Visualized on an SVG Radar / Spider Chart with percentiles.
Personalized behavioral insights and cognitive strengths breakdown.

sections.name: Personality Types
sections.description: Contrast the dimensional trait approach with categorical type theories. Trace Carl Jung's 1921 work 'Psychological Types', explore archetypes (Persona, Shadow, Anima/Animus, Self), and examine why modern academic psychology favors continuous traits over rigid MBTI categories.
keyPoints: Type vs Trait: Personality exists on continuous bell curves (traits), not binary boxes (types).
The Jungian Shadow: Repressed, unrecognized aspects of self that project onto opponents.
The Barnum / Forer Effect: Why people gullibly believe generic, universally applicable personality descriptions.

thoughtExperiment.title: The Teletransporter Paradox (Derek Parfit)
thoughtExperiment.scenario: A futuristic scanner records every subatomic particle in your body, disintegrates you on Earth, and beams the exact blueprint to Mars where a replication chamber rebuilds you molecule-for-molecule. Did you travel to Mars, or did you die on Earth while a clone woke up?
thoughtExperiment.takeaway: Challenges whether personal identity is an unbroken physical entity or an illusory psychological continuity of memory, personality, and consciousness.

quiz.question: Which of the Big Five personality dimensions reflects an individual's tendency toward organization, self-discipline, and dependability?
quiz.explanation: Conscientiousness describes traits related to impulse control, organization, goal-directed behavior, and persistence.

quiz.question: What is the psychological phenomenon where individuals believe vague, generally positive personality descriptions apply specifically to them?
quiz.explanation: The Barnum (or Forer) Effect explains why astrology and non-scientific personality tests feel eerily accurate by using universal statements.

quiz.question: Why do contemporary academic psychologists prefer the Big Five trait model over the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI)?
options: MBTI is too long to administer
Human traits exist on continuous bell curves rather than artificial either/or dichotomies
MBTI costs too much to compute
The Big Five was invented earlier
quiz.explanation: Personality characteristics are continuous dimensions normally distributed in the population, whereas MBTI forces continuous scores into artificial binary categories.

quiz.question: According to Carl Jung, which archetype represents the hidden, unintegrated, and repressed facets of the psyche?
quiz.explanation: The Jungian Shadow encompasses the instinctual, unacceptable, or suppressed aspects of the personal and collective unconscious.

exhibits.title: Cognitive Bias Room
exhibits.subtitle: Heuristics, common thinking errors, and evolutionary shortcuts of the human mind
exhibits.curatorQuote: We pride ourselves on being logical creatures, yet we are prisoners of ancient cognitive shortcuts designed for survival on the savannah, not modern statistics.
exhibits.description: Step into the chamber of mental traps. Human rationality is bounded: our brains use System 1 fast heuristics that work well enough in nature, but lead to systematic blunders in the modern world. Uncover confirmation bias, anchoring, and the sunk cost fallacy.

sections.name: Common Thinking Errors
sections.description: Kahneman and Tversky documented dozens of systematic deviations from rational judgment. We rely on heuristics—mental shortcuts that ease cognitive burden but generate predictable illusions.
keyPoints: Confirmation Bias: Seeking, favoring, and remembering data that confirms preexisting beliefs while ignoring contradictions.
Availability Heuristic: Overestimating the probability of events that easily spring to mind (e.g. plane crashes vs car accidents).
Anchoring Bias: Over-relying on the first piece of information encountered when making estimates.
Sunk Cost Fallacy: Continuing an endeavor once an investment of money, effort, or time has been made, regardless of current utility.
Dunning-Kruger Effect: Low-ability individuals suffer from illusory superiority, overestimating their competence.

sections.name: Bias Demonstrations
sections.description: Hands-on experiments where you will personally fall into cognitive traps! Try the interactive 2-4-6 Rule discovery game and the Anchoring Price challenge.
keyPoints: Peter Wason's 2-4-6 Hypothesis Task: Test your confirmation bias by guessing the hidden number sequence rule.
Anchoring Price Estimator: See how an arbitrary high or low initial number shifts your financial estimates.
System 1 vs System 2 Conflict: The Bat & Ball riddle ($1.10 total, bat costs $1 more than ball).

sections.name: Real-Life Examples
sections.description: Examine how cognitive biases exert profound consequences across medical diagnoses, courtroom witness testimony, stock market bubbles, and social media polarization.
keyPoints: Medicine: Diagnostic anchoring causes clinicians to overlook rare diseases after initial quick impressions.
Finance: Loss aversion and overconfidence fuel market panic selling and asset bubbles.
Justice System: Confirmation bias leads investigators to build cases around early suspects, ignoring counter-evidence.
Social Media: Algorithmic echo chambers exploit confirmation bias and outrage heuristics to maximize engagement.

thoughtExperiment.title: The Bat and Ball Problem (System 1 vs System 2)
thoughtExperiment.scenario: A bat and a ball together cost $1.10. The bat costs $1.00 more than the ball. How much does the ball cost?
thoughtExperiment.takeaway: Over 80% of university students spontaneously answer $0.10. System 1 offers an intuitive shortcut answer, but simple algebra (System 2) reveals the ball is $0.05 ($1.05 + $0.05 = $1.10).

quiz.question: Which cognitive bias explains why investors hold onto losing stocks to avoid admitting a loss, throwing good money after bad?
quiz.explanation: The Sunk Cost Fallacy compels people to persist in a failing course of action because of unrecoverable resources already committed.

quiz.question: When people drastically overestimate the frequency of shark attacks compared to falling coconuts, which heuristic is primarily responsible?
quiz.explanation: The Availability Heuristic causes people to judge likelihood by how easily vivid, dramatic examples (like news stories of shark attacks) are recalled.

quiz.question: What did Peter Wason's famous '2-4-6' number task demonstrate about human hypothesis testing?
options: People primarily test hypotheses by seeking confirming evidence rather than disconfirming tests
quiz.explanation: Participants repeatedly proposed sequences fitting their narrow hypothesis (e.g. 'evens increasing by 2') rather than attempting tests that would disprove their assumption.

quiz.question: According to Kahneman's dual-process theory, what are the primary characteristics of System 1 thinking?
quiz.explanation: System 1 operates automatically and swiftly with little or no effort, using evolutionary shortcuts and pattern recognition.

exhibits.title: Decision-Making Room
exhibits.subtitle: Probability paradoxes, risk analysis, and logical reasoning dilemmas
exhibits.curatorQuote: Between stimulus and response lies a choice. In that choice lies our human freedom, bounded by our probabilistic blindness.
exhibits.description: Step into the laboratory of choice. Engage with the Monty Hall probability dilemma, explore Kahneman and Tversky's Nobel Prize-winning Prospect Theory, and test your deductive reasoning with the Wason Selection Task.

sections.name: Decision Simulations
sections.description: Interactive decision dilemmas that pit human intuition against mathematical reality. Experience the Monty Hall 3-Door paradox and the classic Trolley Problem.
keyPoints: The Monty Hall Problem: In a 3-door game with 1 prize, switching doors after the host reveals a goat doubles your win probability from 33.3% to 66.7%.
The Trolley Problem: Utilitarian logic (switch track to save 5 and kill 1) vs Deontological moral intuition (refusing to actively push a bystander).
Prisoner's Dilemma: Individual self-interest leads to mutually suboptimal outcomes; iterated versions reward 'Tit-for-Tat'.

sections.name: Risk Analysis
sections.description: Classical economics assumed humans are rational utility maximizers. Kahneman and Tversky's Prospect Theory showed that human risk decisions are governed by psychological reference points and loss aversion.
keyPoints: Loss Aversion: Losses loom roughly 2 to 2.5 times larger than equivalent gains (losing $100 feels worse than winning $100 feels good).
Framing Effect: People are risk-averse when options are framed as gains ('200 lives saved') but risk-seeking when framed as losses ('400 people will die').
Certainty Effect: People disproportionately overvalue absolute certainty compared to high probability.

sections.name: Logical Thinking Activities
sections.description: Hands-on deductive and formal reasoning puzzles. Engage with the Wason 4-Card Selection Task and syllogistic validity tests.
keyPoints: Wason Selection Task: Test the rule 'If a card has a vowel, it has an even number on the other side' (testing cards [A, D, 4, 7]).
Only ~10% of people select the logically correct cards (A and 7, testing modus ponens and modus tollens).
Evolutionary Social Contract: When framed as a social rule ('Drinking beer requires age 21+'), accuracy skyrockets to over 75%!

thoughtExperiment.title: The Asian Disease Problem (Framing Paradox)
thoughtExperiment.scenario: An unusual disease is expected to kill 600 people. Program A saves 200 people for sure. Program B has a 1/3 chance that 600 people are saved and 2/3 chance no one is saved. When presented this way, 72% choose A (risk-averse). But when presented as: Program C causes 400 people to die, Program D has 1/3 chance nobody dies and 2/3 chance 600 die, 78% choose D (risk-seeking)!
thoughtExperiment.takeaway: Human risk appetite flips 180 degrees purely based on linguistic framing—gain vs loss—despite identical mathematical outcomes.

quiz.question: In the classic Monty Hall problem with 3 doors, what happens to your win probability if you choose to SWITCH after the host opens a goat door?
quiz.explanation: Your original door had a 1/3 chance of being correct. The remaining unchosen doors had a combined 2/3 chance, which collapses entirely onto the remaining unopened door once Monty reveals a goat.

quiz.question: According to Prospect Theory, approximately how much more painful is a financial loss compared to an equivalent financial gain?
options: Roughly twice as intense (2 to 2.5 times)
quiz.explanation: Empirical experiments demonstrate that loss aversion causes losses to psychologically sting approximately 2 to 2.5 times more than the pleasure of equivalent gains.

quiz.question: Given 4 cards showing [E, K, 4, 7], which cards MUST you flip to test the rule: 'If a card has a vowel, it has an even number on the back'?
quiz.explanation: You must flip 'E' (vowel) to verify it has an even number (modus ponens), and '7' (odd number) to verify it does NOT have a vowel (modus tollens). Flipping 4 does not test the rule because the rule does not state even numbers only belong to vowels.

quiz.question: Herbert Simon introduced which Nobel Prize-winning concept to describe how humans settle for satisfactory decisions rather than computing optimal ones?
quiz.explanation: Herbert Simon coined 'Satisficing' within Bounded Rationality—humans seek solutions that meet a threshold of adequacy due to limited time and processing power.

exhibits.title: Brain Lab / AI Guide Room
exhibits.subtitle: Interactive neuroscience laboratory, neural mapping, and AI psychology docent
exhibits.curatorQuote: The human brain is the most complex structure in the known universe: 86 billion neurons, each connected to thousands of others, forming a network with more synaptic states than atoms in the galaxy.
exhibits.description: Welcome to the central nexus of the museum. Here, human psychology meets modern computational neuroscience and artificial intelligence. Consult your AI Guide Dr. Sophia Vance for deep pedagogical explanations, test your knowledge in the Psychology Q&A repository, and explore neuroplasticity.

sections.name: AI-Powered Explanations
sections.description: Dr. Sophia Vance is an interactive cognitive guide capable of explaining any psychological concept, synthesizing debates between historical psychoanalysis and contemporary neurobiology, and providing customized explanations suited to your learning level.
keyPoints: Ask any question regarding psychology, neuropsychology, cognitive biases, or mental wellness.
Synthesizes classical psychology (Freud, Jung, Skinner) with modern fMRI and connectome neuroscience.
Context-aware: Dr. Sophia follows you into any museum room to provide instant exhibit breakdowns.

sections.name: Psychology Q&A
sections.description: Curated interactive repository of foundational psychology inquiries, breakthrough experiments (Milgram, Stanford Prison, Phineas Gage, Little Albert), and neuroscience FAQs.
keyPoints: Searchable and categorized across Cognitive, Social, Clinical, and Developmental Psychology.
Case Studies: Phineas Gage (prefrontal damage and personality), Patient H.M. (hippocampus and memory).
Neurotransmitter guide: Dopamine, Serotonin, GABA, Glutamate, Acetylcholine, and Endorphins.

thoughtExperiment.title: The Chinese Room Argument (John Searle)
thoughtExperiment.scenario: A person who understands no Chinese sits in a closed room with a rulebook. English instructions tell them: 'When given Chinese character X, reply with Chinese character Y.' To someone outside, the room appears fluent in Chinese. Does the person inside understand Chinese?
thoughtExperiment.takeaway: Searle argued that syntax (symbol manipulation) does not equal semantics (true intentional understanding), raising deep questions about AI and human consciousness.

quiz.question: Who is celebrated as the father of modern neuroscience for discovering that neurons are individual discrete cells rather than a continuous net?
quiz.explanation: Santiago Ramón y Cajal proved the 'Neuron Doctrine' using Golgi silver staining, demonstrating that neurons are discrete individual signaling units.

quiz.question: What famous 1848 railroad worker's accidental frontal lobe injury provided the earliest evidence that the prefrontal cortex governs social behavior and personality?
quiz.explanation: Phineas Gage survived an iron rod through his ventromedial prefrontal cortex, which transformed his personality from polite and reliable to profane and impulsive.

quiz.question: Which primary neurotransmitter is predominantly responsible for voluntary muscle activation and memory consolidation in the hippocampus?
quiz.explanation: Acetylcholine (ACh) is essential for motor neuron signaling at neuromuscular junctions and plays a key role in hippocampal memory encoding.

quiz.question: What does the term 'Neuroplasticity' describe in contemporary brain science?
options: The brain is made of synthetic polymer compounds
The brain's ability to reorganize neural pathways and synaptic connections throughout life
The irreversible hardening of brain tissue in adulthood
The speed of electrical conduction along axons
quiz.explanation: Neuroplasticity refers to the brain's dynamic capacity to rewire synaptic connections, form new circuits, and adapt structurally in response to experience and learning.

journalEntries.title: Reflections on Sensory Gating and Top-Down Perception
journalEntries.content: Watching visitors interact with the Müller-Lyer and Hermann Grid illusions reminded me how fragile our grasp of objective reality is. We inhabit a simulation crafted by evolutionary pressures.

aiDocentProfiles.name: Dr. Sophia Vance
aiDocentProfiles.title: Senior AI Neuro-Curator & Cognitive Guide
aiDocentProfiles.systemPersonality: Intellectually profound, compassionate, articulate, blending historical psychology (Freud, Jung, James, Kahneman) with cutting-edge neuroscience (fMRI, predictive processing, connectomics). Welcomes visitors with warmth, answers questions, and grounds complex phenomena into unforgettable metaphors.
